universalGuides.label: Weekly focus
prompts: If they remember only one sentence next week, what should it be?
What replay evidence makes this the right focus now?
What can they repeat in one ordinary ladder session without you present?
What are you intentionally leaving alone this week?
universalGuides.structure: One focus → one reason → one exact action → one reflection question → one protected boundary

universalGuides.label: Worksheet
prompts: What should the student notice before you explain it?
Which plausible wrong answer would reveal a real misconception?
What tradeoff should they explain in their own words?
What replay evidence would prove the lesson transferred into play?

universalGuides.label: Session notes
prompts: What became clearer during this session?
What is still uncertain?
What should the student keep doing exactly as-is?
What changes in the next practice block?
How will both of you know the change worked?
universalGuides.insertableStructure:
KEEP

CHANGE

NEXT REP

SUCCESS LOOKS LIKE

REVIEW AFTER

universalGuides.label: Voice memo
prompts: Which single moment would you pause?
What cue was available on screen before the outcome?
Can you turn the advice into one if/then rule?
What should they repeat in their next three games?
What did they already do well that should stay intact?
recordingGuide: 85–90 sec · End with what to keep
universalGuides.starterScript: Here’s the one moment I want you to remember: ___. The cue available before it was ___. Next time, if you see ___, then ___. Practice that decision for the next ___ games. Keep doing ___—we are sharpening one choice, not rebuilding everything.

universalGuides.label: Video
prompts: What should already be visible before your first sentence?
Which short clip shows the cause, not only the result?
Where can you pause and ask the student to predict the next decision?
What exact practice rep should close the video?
universalGuides.structure: SHOW IT → PAUSE IT → EXPLAIN THE RULE → REHEARSE THE NEXT REP

universalGuides.label: Annotated screenshot
prompts: Circle the cue that should attract attention first.
Use one arrow to show the danger or opportunity.
Label the action the cue should trigger.
Remove any mark that does not change a decision.
universalGuides.helperCopy: Aim for one cue, one consequence, and one action. A clean frame teaches faster than a fully marked map.

universalGuides.label: Replay note
prompts: Which timestamp contains the trigger?
Which timestamp contains the decision?
Which timestamp makes the consequence visible?
What should the student rehearse mentally before the next game?
universalGuides.insertableStructure:
TRIGGER · [timestamp] — What became knowable

CHOICE · [timestamp] — The decision that mattered

CONSEQUENCE · [timestamp] — What the choice created

NEXT TIME — One replacement rule

universalGuides.label: PDF practice card
prompts: Can the useful part fit on one page?
What is the single goal?
Which three cues matter most?
What is the if/then decision rule?
What drill and measurement make improvement visible?
universalGuides.insertableStructure:
GOAL
WHY IT MATTERS
THREE CUES
IF / THEN RULE
PRACTICE REP
SUCCESS MEASURE

universalGuides.label: Custom build
prompts: What problem is this build designed to solve?
Where is its first real decision fork?
Which benchmark is a health check rather than a vanity timing?
What is the safest recovery when the opening is disrupted?
What must the student scout before following the script blindly?

worksheetTemplates.title: Session prep — bring one useful problem
worksheetTemplates.description: Helps the student arrive with evidence, context, and one question worth solving.
coachPrompts: Which recurring decision is worth spending session time on?
Which replays show the ordinary pattern rather than an extreme result?
What should the student be able to do without you after this session?

blocks.q: How clear is the main problem you want help with? 1 = “I only know the result was bad.” 10 = “I can name the moment, cue, and decision.”
Describe one situation that kept repeating. What did you expect to happen, and what happened instead?
What information did you have before the decision? Separate what you saw from what you assumed.
Attach up to three representative replays. Include an ordinary game—not only your cleanest win or worst loss.
What would make this session feel useful when you return to ladder?

worksheetTemplates.title: Weekly check-in — signal, not diary
worksheetTemplates.description: A short check-in that surfaces transfer, confusion, and the next useful coaching decision.
coachPrompts: What evidence would show last week’s focus transferring into play?
Does the current difficulty need a clearer cue, a tighter rule, or more repetition?
What should remain unchanged while the next skill develops?

blocks.q: What single focus did you practice, and roughly how many games did you give it?
Name one cue you noticed earlier than you would have last week.
Where did your plan become unclear? Describe the first uncertain moment, not only the final loss.
What does this focus need next?
Attach one replay that best represents the week. Representative matters more than impressive.

worksheetTemplates.title: Build understanding — explain the branches
worksheetTemplates.description: Checks whether the student understands the build as a decision system, not a memorized list.
coachPrompts: Which branch is the student memorizing without understanding?
What visible cue makes that branch necessary?
What recovery is both safe and realistic when execution breaks?

blocks.q: What position is this build trying to create, and what makes that position useful?
Where is the first scouting-dependent branch? Name the cue and the response.
Which benchmark tells you the build is healthy? What usually caused it to miss?
What part of the build is flexible, and what part should remain stable?
If the opening is disrupted, what is the safest playable recovery?
Attach one clean execution and one disrupted execution of this build.

worksheetTemplates.title: Replay review — evidence before verdict
worksheetTemplates.description: Moves the student from “I lost because…” toward observable cause and a reusable rule.
coachPrompts: What is the earliest actionable cause rather than the final symptom?
Which belief can the replay confirm or disprove?
What one reusable if/then rule should emerge from the review?

blocks.q: Before opening the replay, what do you currently believe decided the game?
Find the first moment the game became harder. What changed, and what evidence was visible just before it?
What were your realistic options at that moment?
Which option did you choose, and what tradeoff came with it?
After reviewing the evidence, what part of your original explanation changed?
Finish this rule: “Next time, if I see ___, I will ___ because ___.”

template.title: PvP decision lab — information before commitment
template.description: A build-neutral decision worksheet. It teaches the student to separate observed information from assumptions and submit representative evidence.
coachPrompts: Which commitment happened before the student had enough information?
What was the smallest safe response supported by the known facts?
Which cue should trigger the correct branch next game?

blocks.q: Before your first irreversible commitment—extra Gateways, tech, or a Nexus—what information did you have, and what were you still assuming?
Which cue most changed your plan?
opts: Gateway or unit count at the front
A missing probe or possible proxy path
The first tech or specialist-unit reveal
I changed course without a clear cue

blocks.q: Write a one-sentence response rule for each branch: one-base pressure, early expansion, and hidden tech.
Choose one engagement or defense. What space did you need to control, which unit could not be lost, and what would make you disengage?
How confidently can you distinguish pressure from greed before committing? 1 = guessing; 10 = I can name the cues and my response.
Attach 2–3 PvP replays using the same opening: one clean win, one loss, and—if available—one game where you felt uncertain. Do not cherry-pick.

voice.title: PvP — commit after information
voice.script: Quick PvP rule: do not let uncertainty force the biggest commitment. Before extra Gateways, tech, or a Nexus, separate what you saw from what you fear. Classify the position as pressure, expansion, or hidden tech, then choose the smallest safe response that keeps your plan alive. For the next three PvPs, say the cue and your branch out loud when you commit.

assignment.title: Prove the branch before committing
assignment.action: Play three PvPs with one opening. After each game, record the first reliable cue, the branch you chose, and whether the replay supports that choice.

template.title: PvT decision lab — economy, production, movement
template.description: A build-neutral decision worksheet. It teaches the student to separate observed information from assumptions and submit representative evidence.
coachPrompts: Which read was missing: economy, production, or movement?
Did the response match the visible threat or the fear of one?
What preparation would make the next commitment reversible?

blocks.q: At your first reliable scouting moment, what did Terran show in three categories: economy, production, and movement? Separate visible facts from inference.
Which cue most changed your plan?
opts: Units leaving the Terran side of the map
My scout was denied and I filled the gap with an assumption

blocks.q: Write your response rule for early pressure, a standard bio setup, and economic or tech greed.
Before your first major move-out or defense, what provided vision, what was your retreat route, and where would reinforcements enter?
How confidently can you identify Terran’s plan before its first committed move-out? 1 = reacting after contact; 10 = reading the setup from evidence.
Attach 2–3 PvT replays with the same opening. Include one game where your first read was correct and one where your read or response broke down.

voice.title: PvT — read three columns
voice.script: Quick PvT rule: read Terran in three columns—economy, production, and movement. A natural tells one part of the story, add-ons and unit count tell another, and units leaving the base make it urgent. Before committing to tech or a move-out, name one fact from each column. For the next three PvTs, record the first cue that changed your plan.

assignment.title: Read economy, production, movement
assignment.action: Play three PvTs. Before your first major commitment, name one confirmed fact about Terran economy, production, and unit movement.

template.title: PvZ decision lab — pressure without losing the map
template.description: A build-neutral decision worksheet. It teaches the student to separate observed information from assumptions and submit representative evidence.
coachPrompts: What specific result was the pressure meant to buy?
Which Zerg cues best separated worker production from units?
What cost at home made the pressure unprofitable?

blocks.q: At your first reliable read, record what you actually saw about the Zerg third, gas mining, visible Queens or lings, and drone saturation. What remained unknown?
Which cue most changed your plan?
opts: My scouting unit was denied before confirming anything

blocks.q: Write your response rule for an early all-in, low-drone pressure, and normal macro or greed.
What result makes your pressure worthwhile? If it deals no direct damage, which economy, tech, and defensive coverage must remain safe?
How confidently can you tell when Zerg is building workers versus units? 1 = judging after the attack arrives; 10 = using several confirmed cues.
Attach 2–3 PvZ replays with the same opening. Include one game where pressure created value and one where the pressure cost too much at home.

voice.title: PvZ — pressure with a home plan
voice.script: Quick PvZ rule: pressure is only good when you know what it is buying. Before moving out, decide what result you want and what must stay safe at home if no damage happens. Read the third, gas, units, and drone saturation together. For the next three PvZs, name your pressure goal before crossing the map and review whether you left on time.

assignment.title: Give pressure a purpose and an exit
assignment.action: Play three PvZs with the same opening. Before moving out, name the result you want, what must remain safe at home, and the condition that makes you leave.

template.title: ZvP decision lab — drone with evidence
template.description: A build-neutral decision worksheet. It teaches the student to separate observed information from assumptions and submit representative evidence.
coachPrompts: Which confirmed cue should stop drones, and which should restart them?
Where can follow-up scouting reliably confirm the Protoss branch?
Was the response based on visible tech or an untested fear?

blocks.q: From your Overlord and follow-up scouting, what did you confirm about the Nexus, Gateway pressure, gas usage, tech path, and possible proxy space?
Which cue most changed your plan?
opts: A second gas or early tech clue
Scouting was denied before I confirmed a branch

blocks.q: Write your response rule for early Gateway pressure, Oracle or Adept pressure, and a greedy third or tech setup.
At what evidence did you stop droning and make units? Was that trigger visible in the replay, or was it based on fear?
How confidently can you choose a drone ceiling from scouting information? 1 = mostly instinct; 10 = I can name the cue and production response.
Attach 2–3 ZvP replays. Include one where your drone-to-unit decision felt correct and one where you were too greedy or too defensive.

voice.title: ZvP — drone from evidence
voice.script: Quick ZvP rule: every extra drone should be supported by information. Use Nexus timing, Gateway-unit count, gas, and tech clues together instead of reacting to one scary possibility. Decide what exact cue stops drones and what cue starts them again. For the next three ZvPs, write down the evidence behind both decisions.

assignment.title: Drone from confirmed information
assignment.action: Play three ZvPs. Record the cue that stopped drones and the cue that started them again, then verify both decisions in the replay.

template.title: ZvT decision lab — connect production to drone safety
template.description: A build-neutral decision worksheet. It teaches the student to separate observed information from assumptions and submit representative evidence.
coachPrompts: Which Terran production cue defines the safe drone window?
How can Queens, creep, and vision buy more decision time?
Did the defense preserve the macro engine or interrupt it?

blocks.q: What did the first Reaper, Overlord path, or follow-up scout confirm about Terran’s expansion, Factory add-on, reactor production, Starport, and Hellion count?
Which cue most changed your plan?
opts: Scouting was denied and I guessed

blocks.q: Write your response rule for one-base pressure, Hellion-based pressure into air or bio, and a fast third or mech setup.
Pick one defensive cycle. How did Queens, creep, vision, and unit positioning protect drones without overproducing defense?
How confidently can you connect Terran production to a safe drone window? 1 = reacting on arrival; 10 = adjusting from confirmed production.
Attach 2–3 ZvT replays. Include one where your drone window was correct and one where your economy or defense became unbalanced.

voice.title: ZvT — connect production to safety
voice.script: Quick ZvT rule: Terran production tells you when drones are safe. Connect expansion timing, Factory setup, Hellion count, and Starport information to one production response. Queens, creep, and positioning should buy information as well as defense. For the next three ZvTs, name the production cue before changing your drone plan.

assignment.title: Connect Terran production to drone safety
assignment.action: Play three ZvTs. Before changing drone production, name the Terran production or movement cue that justified the change.

template.title: ZvZ decision lab — set the drone ceiling deliberately
template.description: A build-neutral decision worksheet. It teaches the student to separate observed information from assumptions and submit representative evidence.
coachPrompts: Which evidence supports the student’s chosen drone ceiling?
What cue should make units, and what cue should allow drones again?
Did the opponent truly commit or only threaten aggression?

blocks.q: What did you confirm about the opponent’s natural, gas, pool timing, ling count, Baneling Nest, and drone count before choosing your own drone ceiling?
Which cue most changed your plan?
Write your response rule for a ling flood, ling-bane pressure, and a fast third or economic opening.
Name the exact cue that allowed you to drone again. If there was no cue, what information should you seek next time?
How confidently can you distinguish real aggression from pressure that only threatens aggression? 1 = always guessing; 10 = using economy, gas, and unit evidence together.
Attach 2–3 ZvZ replays with the same opening. Include one stable early game and one where your drone or unit decision became unclear.

voice.title: ZvZ — choose the drone ceiling
voice.script: Quick ZvZ rule: do not discover your drone ceiling by getting attacked. Read the natural, gas, ling count, and Baneling information together, then choose the number deliberately. Set one cue that makes units and another that allows drones again. For the next three ZvZs, compare that rule with what the replay actually showed.

assignment.title: Choose the drone ceiling deliberately
assignment.action: Play three ZvZs with one opening. Set your drone ceiling from visible economy, gas, and unit cues; review whether those cues were accurate.

template.title: TvP decision lab — move out with a complete picture
template.description: A build-neutral decision worksheet. It teaches the student to separate observed information from assumptions and submit representative evidence.
coachPrompts: Which move-out checklist item was missing before commitment?
Which Protoss branch did the available evidence support?
What retreat or counterattack condition needed an answer?

blocks.q: From the SCV, Reaper, scan, or first contact, what did you confirm about Protoss economy, Gateway units, gas usage, tech clues, and possible proxy space?
Which cue most changed your plan?
opts: I moved out without enough information

blocks.q: Write your response rule for one-base or proxy pressure, fast tech pressure, and a standard expansion or greedy setup.
Before your move-out, what was your detection plan, reinforcement path, retreat condition, and answer to a counterattack or warp-in?
How confidently can you distinguish Protoss pressure from tech or economy before committing units? 1 = learning on contact; 10 = acting from confirmed clues.
Attach 2–3 TvP replays with the same opening. Include one move-out that had a clear purpose and one where information or preparation was missing.

voice.title: TvP — prepare the move-out
voice.script: Quick TvP rule: a move-out needs more than enough units. Before leaving, name your information, detection, reinforcement path, retreat condition, and answer to a counterattack. Protoss pressure, tech, and greed require different preparation. For the next three TvPs, pause mentally before moving out and confirm those five pieces.

assignment.title: Complete the move-out checklist
assignment.action: Play three TvPs. Before each committed move-out, confirm information, detection, reinforcement path, retreat condition, and counterattack coverage.

template.title: TvT decision lab — vision creates the siege advantage
template.description: A build-neutral decision worksheet. It teaches the student to separate observed information from assumptions and submit representative evidence.
coachPrompts: What source of vision supported the siege decision?
Which zone and reinforcement timing mattered most?
What exit condition would have prevented overextension?

blocks.q: What did your Reaper, scan, or early units confirm about gas count, expansion timing, Factory or Starport setup, and mobile-unit count?
Which cue most changed your plan?
opts: I committed without a reliable read

blocks.q: Write your response rule for proxy or one-base air pressure, a fast expansion, and a Tank-based push or greedy setup.
Choose one siege sequence. What gave vision, which zone had to remain controlled, and what was the exit condition before you advanced?
How confidently can you judge when to advance, hold, or reposition a siege line? 1 = deciding after contact; 10 = using vision and reinforcement timing.
Attach 2–3 TvT replays. Include one game where vision supported your positioning and one where you moved or sieged with incomplete information.

voice.title: TvT — vision before position
voice.script: Quick TvT rule: vision creates the siege advantage. Before advancing, know what grants vision, which zone your Tanks must control, where reinforcements arrive, and what makes you reposition. Do not confuse moving forward with gaining value. For the next three TvTs, review the ten seconds before every major siege decision.

assignment.title: Create vision before advancing
assignment.action: Play three TvTs. Review the ten seconds before each siege-line move and identify what vision, reinforcement timing, and exit condition supported it.

template.title: TvZ decision lab — give every move-out a purpose
template.description: A build-neutral decision worksheet. It teaches the student to separate observed information from assumptions and submit representative evidence.
coachPrompts: What single purpose was the move-out meant to serve?
Which Zerg economy or unit cues justified that purpose?
When did the purpose stop being safely achievable?

blocks.q: What did the first Reaper, scan, or pressure unit confirm about Hatchery timing, gas, pool, third base, ling count, and early creep spread?
Which cue most changed your plan?
opts: I followed my build without updating the read

blocks.q: Write your response rule for early ling or Roach pressure, a normal macro setup, and an unusually greedy economy or fast tech.
Give your next move-out one primary purpose: clear creep, force units, deny economy, threaten tech, or finish the game. What makes you leave safely if that purpose is no longer achievable?
How confidently can you tell whether pressure is creating value without forcing direct damage? 1 = measuring only kills; 10 = tracking creep, units, economy, and map access.
Attach 2–3 TvZ replays. Include one purposeful move-out and one where pressure stayed too long or had no clear objective.

voice.title: TvZ — purpose before pressure
voice.script: Quick TvZ rule: every move-out needs one primary purpose—clear creep, force units, deny economy, threaten tech, or finish the game. Decide that purpose before crossing the map and leave when it is no longer achievable. For the next three TvZs, state the purpose first and grade the move-out by that purpose, not only by kills.

assignment.title: Give every move-out one purpose
assignment.action: Play three TvZs. State the move-out’s primary purpose before crossing the map, then grade it by that purpose rather than kills alone.
